title: Using AI Tools Wisely
summary: Understand what generative AI can and cannot do, write good prompts, check the answers, and use it honestly and safely for learning.

lessons.title: What generative AI is and is not

body.p: Generative AI tools, such as chatbots that write text, are computer programs trained on very large amounts of writing. They learn patterns in language, and when you type a request they produce a response by predicting, word by word, what text is likely to fit. This is why they can write an email, explain a topic or summarise a passage in a few seconds.

list: It predicts; it does not look things up the way you check a textbook. A fluent answer is not the same as a true answer.
It can be confidently wrong. It may state a false date, a wrong formula or a made-up fact in the same calm tone as a correct one.
It can invent sources. People have been given book titles, quotations, court cases and web links that look real but do not exist. This is often called hallucination.
It does not understand you the way a teacher does. It does not know your syllabus, your teacher's marking style or your life unless you tell it, and it can still ignore what you tell it.
Its knowledge has limits. It may not know recent events, local rules or your exam board's current requirements.

check.q: An AI chatbot answers in a calm, confident tone. What does that tell you about whether the answer is correct?
o: Nothing on its own: it writes just as confidently when it is wrong
It is very likely to be correct
It checked a database before answering
check.e: The tool predicts likely text, so it sounds equally sure when it is right and when it is wrong. Tone is not evidence.

body.p: Chidi asks an AI tool for three journal articles on school feeding programmes in West Africa, with authors and years. The tool returns three impressive-looking references. When Chidi searches his library database, two of the articles do not exist, and the third exists but has a different author. The tool produced references that look like real ones because that is what such text usually looks like. Chidi learns an important rule: never cite a source you have not found and opened yourself.

AI can be a helpful assistant for brainstorming ideas, explaining a concept in simpler words, giving examples, quizzing you, checking your grammar, or turning your messy notes into a tidy outline. It is weaker when accuracy matters, when the answer depends on local or very recent facts, or when judgement and ethics are needed. The safest way to think about it is as a fast but unreliable helper: useful, but not an authority.

check.q: Which task plays to an AI tool's strengths?
o: Telling you today's exact exchange rate
Turning your messy notes into a tidy outline
Confirming that a journal article exists
check.e: Rewording and organising text you supply is what these tools do well. Live facts and references must be checked at the source.

body.tip: Treat every AI answer as a draft written by someone who sounds sure but may be wrong. You are responsible for what you use.

body.p: A prompt is the instruction you type to an AI tool. The quality of what you get back depends heavily on the quality of what you ask. Vague prompts give vague answers. Clear prompts make the tool's job easier and save your time.

body.h: Five parts of a good prompt

list: Role: who the tool should act as, for example 'a patient Biology tutor for a 16-year-old'.
Task: exactly what you want done, such as 'explain', 'quiz me', 'give feedback on'.
Context: the background, such as your level, syllabus, deadline, or the text you are working on.
Format: the shape of the answer, such as 'five bullet points', 'a table', 'under 150 words', 'simple English'.
Examples: a sample of the style or answer you want, so the tool can copy the pattern.

body.p: Weak prompt: 'Tell me about photosynthesis.' This could return anything, at any level, of any length.

body.code:
Act as a patient Biology tutor for a 16-year-old preparing for school-leaving exams.
Explain photosynthesis in simple English.
Use the word equation, then three short steps.
Finish with three practice questions, without answers, so I can test myself.
Keep it under 200 words.

body.p: The second prompt gives role, task, context and format. The output will usually be much closer to what the learner needs. If the first answer is not right, you can follow up: 'Make it simpler', 'Give a Nigerian/Kenyan/Ghanaian example', or 'You said X; explain why'. Iterating in small steps often works better than one huge prompt.

check.q: What is missing from this prompt: 'Explain photosynthesis in three short steps, then give me two practice questions'?
o: The task
The format
The role and context: who the tool should act as and your level
check.e: The task (explain) and the format (three steps, two questions) are there. It does not say who the tool should act as or what level you are at.

steps: Say who you are and your level, but do not include private details.
Paste only the text you need and say what to do with it.
Ask for the answer in steps if the task is complicated.
Ask the tool to say when it is unsure or when it needs more information.
Read the answer critically and ask follow-up questions.

body.p: Worked example: Amara wants feedback on her essay introduction. She writes: 'Act as an English teacher. Here is my introduction (pasted). Give me three specific strengths and three specific improvements. Do not rewrite it for me.' By saying 'do not rewrite it', she keeps the work her own and uses the tool as a coach.

check.q: The first answer is too advanced for you. What is the best follow-up?
o: 'Make it simpler, for a first-year student, with one everyday example'
Start a new chat and type exactly the same prompt
Accept it and read it twice
check.e: A follow-up that says what to change, and for whom, steers the tool. Repeating the same prompt usually gives a similar answer.

body.tip: If you ask the tool to explain its reasoning or to show steps, you can check each step rather than trusting the final answer.

body.p: Because AI can be wrong while sounding certain, verification is not optional. The more important the use, the more you must check. A casual brainstorm needs little checking. A homework answer, a medical question, a legal point or a number in a report needs a lot.

steps: Identify the claims that matter: facts, numbers, dates, names, quotations, formulas.
Check the important ones in a reliable source: your textbook, class notes, the exam board's syllabus, a government or university website, or an official dataset.
For any source the tool names, search for it yourself. If you cannot find it, do not use it.
Check numbers and calculations yourself. AI tools can make arithmetic and logic mistakes.
Ask a second, independent source or a teacher when stakes are high.
Reject, correct or rewrite whatever you cannot confirm.

list: Very precise statistics with no source.
Quotations attributed to famous people without a named place they were said.
References with real-sounding names that you cannot find.
Answers that contradict your textbook or class notes.
Answers that agree with whatever you suggest, even if you made a mistake. Tools can be too eager to please.

check.q: Which AI answer needs the most careful checking?
o: Five ideas for a birthday party
A medicine dose for a relative
A catchier title for your poster
check.e: Use the harm test: if a wrong dose is harmful, check it with a pharmacist, doctor or the official leaflet.

body.p: Kwame asks an AI tool to solve a Mathematics problem and gets an answer of 48. He does not trust it blindly. He checks by substituting the answer back into the original equation, and it does not work. He asks the tool to show each step, spots where it multiplied wrongly, and fixes it himself to get 42. The check took two minutes and prevented a lost mark. In another case, Esi asks about the symptoms of a health condition. She uses the answer only as a starting point, then reads a health ministry or national health service website and speaks to a nurse before acting.

A good test is: 'If this is wrong, who is harmed, and how badly?' The bigger the harm, the stronger the checking. You should also avoid using AI as your only source for exam preparation, because exam boards test your own understanding, not the tool's.

check.q: A tool solves an equation and gives x = 4. What is the quickest reliable check?
o: Ask the same tool whether it is sure
Ask two other tools and accept the answer that appears twice
Substitute x = 4 back into the original equation
check.e: Substituting back tests the answer directly. Asking tools to agree does not prove anything, because they can share the same mistake.

body.tip: Use AI to produce a first draft and your own checking to make it trustworthy.

lessons.title: Using AI to learn without cheating

body.p: Schools, colleges and universities all want students to learn, and assessments exist to show what you can do yourself. Handing in work that an AI wrote and presenting it as your own is a form of cheating, usually called plagiarism or academic misconduct, and it can lead to lost marks, failing a course or worse. It also cheats you out of the skills the course is meant to give.

body.h: First rule: follow the rules you are given

body.p: Rules differ between schools, courses and even individual assignments. Some teachers allow AI for brainstorming but not for writing. Some ban it entirely for coursework or exams. Exam boards have their own strict rules about what you may use in non-exam assessment. If you are unsure, ask your teacher before you use it. 'I did not know' is a weak defence.

list: Ask it to explain a hard idea in a different way, then test yourself without it.
Ask it to make practice questions from your own notes, and mark yourself.
Ask it to give feedback on your own draft, with suggestions rather than a rewrite.
Ask it to help you plan a study timetable.
Ask it to show a worked example, then solve a similar problem on your own.

check.q: Which use supports your learning rather than replacing it?
o: Asking for practice questions from your notes, then marking yourself
Asking it to write your reflection paragraph
Asking it to reword a classmate's essay for you to submit
check.e: Practice questions make you do the thinking. The other two hand in work that is not yours.

body.h: Uses that usually cross the line

list: Submitting AI-written essays, code or answers as your own.
Using it in a closed-book test or exam when it is not allowed.
Using AI to rewrite your essay so that it escapes detection.
Copying sources that the tool listed without reading them.

body.p: When AI is permitted, be honest about it. A short note works, for example: 'I used an AI tool to generate practice questions and to check the grammar of my second paragraph. All ideas, analysis and final wording are my own.' Keep your prompts and drafts, because they show your process if anyone asks questions.

Worked example: Zainab is allowed by her teacher to use AI for brainstorming. She asks for five angles on an essay about water access, picks two, and writes the essay herself using library sources. She adds a declaration line to her submission. Her classmate Tunde pastes the whole question and submits the result. When the teacher asks Tunde to explain a paragraph, he cannot. Zainab learned the topic and kept her integrity; Tunde risks a penalty and learned nothing.

check.q: Where do you find out whether AI is allowed for a particular assignment?
o: The AI tool's own website
The assignment brief, or your teacher or lecturer
Whatever most classmates are doing
check.e: Rules differ between courses and even between assignments, so the brief and the person who set it decide.

body.tip: Test yourself: could you explain and defend every sentence in the work out loud, without the tool? If not, you have not learned it yet.

body.p: Using AI tools responsibly means thinking about what you give them, what they give back, and whose work is involved.

body.h: Privacy: be careful what you paste

body.p: Treat anything you type into an AI tool as something that may be stored, read by the provider, or used in ways you do not control, depending on the tool's settings and policy. So do not paste personal or confidential information.

list: Never enter passwords, PINs, bank or mobile-money details, or one-time codes.
Avoid ID numbers, home addresses, phone numbers, medical or family details, and exam admission details.
Do not paste another person's private messages, photos or personal data without their permission.
Do not paste confidential school, work or client material such as unreleased exam papers, staff records or business plans unless you are clearly allowed to.
Replace real names with labels such as 'Person A' when you need help with a situation.

check.q: Which of these is safe to paste into an AI tool?
o: Your mobile-money PIN
A screenshot of a friend's private chat
A paragraph you wrote about climate change
check.e: Your own non-personal writing is fine. PINs and other people's private messages should never go in.

body.p: AI learns from human writing, and human writing contains stereotypes and gaps. Tools can therefore produce biased or unfair answers, for example by assuming certain jobs belong to certain genders, or by knowing much less about some countries, languages and cultures than others. If you ask for an example from your own country, the tool may get local details wrong. Notice who is missing, ask for different perspectives, and compare with local sources.

Books, songs, images, articles and software are usually protected by copyright, which means the creator has rights over copying and sharing. An AI tool producing something does not automatically make it free to use. Copying large parts of someone's work, with or without AI, and presenting it as yours is plagiarism, and publishing it may break the law. When using ideas, quotations or images in your work, find the original and cite it. Rules about AI-made material vary between countries and are still changing, so check your school's or country's guidance for anything you will publish or sell.

Worked example: Ife wants help writing to a friend who has been unkind. Instead of pasting the friend's full name and private messages, she writes: 'My friend (Person A) said something hurtful. Help me write a calm reply, with no names or personal details.' She gets the help without exposing anyone's information.

check.q: Why can AI answers be biased?
o: They learn from human writing, which contains stereotypes and gaps
They are deliberately programmed to prefer some groups
Bias only appears when you write in another language
check.e: The tools reflect the writing they learned from, including its stereotypes and its gaps about some places and languages.

body.tip: Before you paste, ask: would I be happy for a stranger to read this?

lessons.title: Deciding when not to use AI

body.p: Knowing when to put the tool down is as important as knowing how to use it. A good user asks first: is AI right for this job?

steps: Am I allowed? Check the rules for the task, school or exam.
Is the purpose to learn this skill myself? If yes, do it first and use AI later, if at all.
Does the task involve private or confidential information? If yes, do not paste it.
Would a wrong answer cause serious harm, such as in health, law, money or safety? If yes, use qualified people and official sources.
Can I check the answer? If I cannot tell whether it is right, I should not rely on it.
Would it be more honest or kind to do this myself, for instance writing a personal apology or a message of sympathy?

body.h: Situations where AI is a poor choice

list: Medical, legal or financial decisions. Speak to a doctor, nurse, lawyer or qualified adviser.
Emergencies. Contact emergency services or a trusted adult.
Exams and tests where tools are banned.
Practising essay writing, problem solving or coding that you need to be able to do alone.
Judging people, such as deciding who is guilty or who deserves a place, based only on a tool's opinion.
Any situation where a human relationship matters, such as comforting a friend.

check.q: Which question should you ask before using AI on a task?
o: Which tool is the fastest?
Am I allowed to use it for this?
How long can the answer be?
check.e: Permission comes first. A fast, long answer is no use if the task does not allow AI.

body.p: If a tool does your thinking every time, your own thinking gets weaker, just as a muscle does when it is never used. A helpful habit is to try first, then ask the tool, and compare. Another is to use it to challenge you: ask it to ask you questions rather than give you answers.

Worked example: Bola has a Chemistry test on Friday. On Tuesday she tries ten past questions by herself and marks them. Then she asks an AI tool to explain the two she got wrong and give three similar questions. On Friday, in the test, no tool is allowed, but she is ready. Her friend Seun asked the tool to solve all ten and read the answers; he felt prepared but struggled in the test because he had never practised thinking it through.
In short: use AI as a helper that you control, with honesty about it, careful checking, protection of private information, and respect for rules and for other people's work.

check.q: Which habit keeps your own skills strong?
o: Ask the tool first so you see the right answer
Use the tool for every step so you never make mistakes
Try the task yourself first, then compare with the tool
check.e: Trying first makes your brain do the work, and comparing afterwards shows you exactly what to fix.

body.tip: Good AI users are not those who use it most, but those who choose well.

quiz.q: An AI tool gives you a neat list of five books for your essay, with authors and years. What should you do before citing them?
options: Look each book up in a library catalogue or reliable database, and cite only those you can find and have opened yourself
Cite all five, because the tool gave authors and years that sound confident and professional enough for an essay
Cite the three whose authors have the most famous-sounding names, since well-known authors are more likely to be real
Cite them all but change the publication years slightly, so the list looks different from what the tool produced

quiz.q: Which statement best describes how a text-generating AI tool works?
options: It looks up each answer in a database of verified facts and then rewrites the result in simpler words
It produces likely-sounding text from patterns learned in large amounts of writing, so it can be fluent but wrong
It understands your syllabus and checks each answer against your exam board's official marking scheme before it replies
It calculates every answer with strict mathematical rules, so numbers and dates it gives are reliably correct

quiz.q: You ask an AI tool to explain Newton's laws and the answer seems clear. Your textbook says something different about one point. What should you do?
options: Trust your textbook and class notes on that point, ask your teacher if unsure, and use the tool only for ideas
Trust the AI answer, because a newer tool has been trained on more recent writing than your older printed textbook has
Average the two answers by combining both versions into one, so that you keep a bit of each source
Write both versions in the exam and hope the examiner marks whichever one matches the marking scheme

quiz.q: Which prompt is most likely to give a useful study aid?
options: 'Water cycle. Give me everything you know about it in one very long answer so I can read it all tonight.'
'Tell me everything about science, and make it as detailed as possible so that I do not need my textbook.'
'Act as a tutor for a 15-year-old. Write five short quiz questions on the water cycle from my notes below, with answers at the end.'
'Do all of my homework for me tonight and write the answers so my teacher will not notice any difference.'

quiz.q: You ask a tool to write a paragraph and the style is not what you wanted. What is the best next step?
options: Give up on the tool and accept the paragraph as it is, since the first answer is the final version
Start a completely new conversation and repeat the same vague request, hoping for a better result this time
Assume the tool cannot change its style once it has written something, so edit every line by hand instead
Reply with specific instructions, such as 'shorter, simpler English, with a local example', and iterate

quiz.q: Your teacher allows AI for brainstorming only. You are writing an essay about renewable energy. Which use is acceptable?
options: Ask for several possible angles on the topic, choose one, and write the essay yourself from your own research
Ask it to write the full essay, then change a few words in each paragraph so it sounds like your style
Ask it to write the essay, then run the text through a rewriting tool so detection software misses it
Ask a friend to put the request to the tool for you, so that the essay is not linked to your account

quiz.q: A classmate suggests using an AI tool during a closed-book exam on your phone because 'nobody will see'. What is the best response?
options: Agree, since the invigilator is not watching closely and a quick look at your phone would be very hard to prove
Refuse, because using it breaks the exam rules and can lead to penalties, and it will not show what you know
Agree, but only for the maths questions, because calculations are simple and the tool is good at doing them
Agree, if you promise to delete the chat afterwards so that nobody can find any record of what you did

quiz.q: Your teacher has allowed AI for checking grammar. You used it for that. How should you handle it in your submission?
options: Say nothing, because grammar checking is a minor kind of help and teachers do not count it as real AI use
Say you used no tools at all, because you wrote every sentence and the tool only fixed a few small errors
Add a short, honest note that you used an AI tool for grammar checking and the ideas and wording are yours
Remove all the corrections before submitting, so that the work looks rougher and nobody suspects any help

quiz.q: You want an AI tool to help you reply to a message, and the message contains your friend's full name, phone number and a private health detail. What is best?
options: Paste everything as it is, so the tool has the full context it needs to write the most suitable reply
Paste the full message, but only if the tool is a famous one that has millions of users around the world
Paste it all, then ask the tool to promise that it will not store or share any of those private details
Replace the name, number and health detail with neutral labels before pasting, or do not paste it at all

quiz.q: Which item should you never type into an AI tool?
options: Your mobile-money PIN or the one-time code that was sent to your phone
A general question about how fractions work and how to add them
A request for a revision timetable that contains no names or personal details
A paragraph of your own opinion about a school topic, with no personal details

quiz.q: You ask an AI tool for a typical day of 'a nurse' and it describes only women, and for 'an engineer' only men. What is the most useful response?
options: Accept it as the real situation in every country, since the tool has read more text than any person could
Recognise this as bias from the data it learned from, ask for varied examples, and check local sources
Report that the tool is broken and stop using AI tools altogether, since one answer proves they are useless
Assume that every answer it gives is the exact opposite of the truth, and do the reverse of what it says

quiz.q: You find a song lyric, a famous article and a photograph and ask an AI tool to 'rewrite them a bit' so you can publish them on your blog as yours. What is the problem?
options: There is no problem, because the AI made the changes, so the new text belongs to you and not the original authors
There is no problem if you change the title and add a line saying you found the material somewhere online
They are likely protected by copyright and presenting them as yours is plagiarism, even if rewritten by AI
There is a problem only if the photographer or songwriter happens to notice and complains about your blog

quiz.q: Your friend has chest pains and asks if an AI tool can say whether it is serious. What is the wisest advice?
options: Let the tool decide whether it is serious, and wait until the morning if it says there is no danger
Ask three different AI tools and go with the majority answer before deciding whether to call anyone
Ask the tool for a home remedy first, and call a nurse only if the pain has not eased after an hour
Seek immediate help from emergency services, a doctor or a trusted adult rather than rely on a tool

quiz.q: Bola has a Chemistry test where tools are not allowed. Which study approach is best?
options: Try questions alone first, then use AI to explain mistakes and make similar practice questions
Ask AI to solve all the past questions for you, then read through the worked answers until you know them
Avoid practising questions and rely on the tool's summaries, since reading them is enough to prepare
Memorise the answers the AI gives, word for word, without trying to understand how they were reached

quiz.q: An AI tool gives a calculation answer of 85 for a budget problem. You are about to put it in your project report. What should you do?
options: Use it as given, because computers are very reliable with arithmetic and the answer looks sensible
Check the working yourself or with a calculator, and fix it before putting it in the report
Round it to the nearest 10 to be safe, since a rounded figure is less likely to contain an error
Use it if the tool says it is confident about the answer and repeats the same figure when asked again
